column1: passwd-fields|F|F1|unix|Which /etc/passwd field identifies a user's numeric primary group?|GID field|Password-placeholder field|Login-shell field|GECOS description field|Account records include distinct identity, group, description, home, and shell fields. The primary group is not a privilege label by itself.|Read a field's role rather than its position vaguely.

shell-nologin|F|F1|unix|An account has a nologin shell. What should not be inferred from that alone?|The account has no usable service-specific authentication path|Interactive shell login is restricted|The shell field affects normal login behavior|Different services may enforce different account policies|A shell restriction can block interactive login without determining every application's use of the account.|Interactive access and service-account authority can differ.

uid-name|F|F2|unix|An account named backup has UID 0. Which fact matters most for its Unix privilege identity?|The numeric UID is the root identity|The friendly name makes it unprivileged|The home path determines its UID|The account's comment cancels UID privileges|Unix identity is numeric. Names can be changed or misleading; effective runtime credentials and other controls still matter.|Do not substitute names for identities.

effective-real|F|F2|unix|Why inspect effective UID as well as real UID after a SUID execution?|Effective credentials govern many permission checks|The real UID is automatically rewritten into the password|Every process has only one identity field|The effective UID exists only for network packets|SUID changes can give a process different effective credentials while retaining its real identity. Exact operations may use different checks.|A process can have several credential fields.

suid-script|F|F2|unix|Why is a SUID bit on a shell script not sufficient evidence of elevation on Linux?|The kernel generally does not honor SUID on scripts|Every script automatically becomes owned by root|Scripts can never execute privileged operations|All script contents are cryptographically verified|Interpreter/script execution rules differ from native executables. Validate the actual mechanism rather than treating a mode bit as proof.|Metadata and runtime semantics must agree.

sticky-directory|F|B13|unix|What does the sticky bit commonly restrict on a shared writable directory?|Who may remove or rename entries they do not own|Who may list every filename in the directory|Who may read the contents of any file|Who may execute every program on the host|Sticky-directory rules constrain entry deletion/renaming, with privileged exceptions. They do not replace file read/write permissions.|Directory-entry protection is not content confidentiality.

sgid-directory|F|B13|unix|What can SGID on a directory commonly influence for newly created children?|Group ownership inheritance|Automatic root ownership of every file|Encryption of every file's contents|The caller's shell password|Directory SGID supports shared group ownership conventions. It does not grant unrestricted root execution.|One special bit can have different effects on files and directories.

acl-mask|F|B13|unix|Why can a named-user ACL entry show more rights than the user's effective access?|The ACL mask may limit the effective rights|The entry is always ignored on Unix|The owner name necessarily overrides every ACL|The file's extension automatically removes write access|POSIX ACL masks constrain certain entries. Tools may show both configured and effective rights.|Declared rights and effective rights can differ.

capability|F|F2|unix|Why inspect file capabilities as well as SUID files on Linux?|Capabilities can grant selected privileged operations without UID 0|Only SUID can grant any privileged operation|Capabilities are a browser cookie format|A capability always grants every root privilege|Capabilities split privileged powers. Their actual grant, bounding conditions, and program behavior matter.|Privilege can be selective rather than all-or-nothing root identity.

cron-consumer|F|F2|unix|A root cron job executes a world-writable helper. What is the central escalation opportunity?|An unprivileged writer controls later privileged code|The file's name reveals the root password|Cron always ignores filesystem permissions|The helper must be reachable over SSH|The scheduler's identity and writable executed material form the path. Confirm timing, environment, and access conditions.|Follow bytes to the identity that consumes them.

path-search|F|F2|unix|A privileged script invokes an unqualified program name from a writable search directory. What should be examined?|Executable search order and control of candidate files|Only the script's comment heading|Only the user's terminal color settings|Only the server's reverse DNS record|An attacker-controlled search path can select unintended code. Absolute paths, environment handling, and permissions affect the risk.|A command name may be resolved through mutable state.

package-backport|F|B14|crest|Why can a distribution package's security revision matter more than its upstream banner?|The distribution may backport fixes|Banners always contain signed patch evidence|Every distribution rewrites all function names|Package metadata grants exploit permission|Vendor package advisories and installed revisions can establish fixes without an upstream version change.|Compare against the vendor's actual maintenance lineage.

ftp-active-passive|F|F3|ftp|In passive FTP, which party connects to the server's advertised data endpoint?|The client|The server to the client listener|The DNS resolver|The SMTP relay|Passive mode changes data-channel direction. The control connection and firewall rules remain separate concerns.|Data and control channels have different flow patterns.

ftp-write-execution|F|F3|ftp|Anonymous upload succeeds into a directory that is not web-served or executed. What is proven?|Anonymous write access, not automatic command execution|Immediate root compromise|A working authenticated SSH shell|The ability to alter every system file|Uploaded files can be risky, but execution needs a relevant consumer or other path. State the observed write boundary accurately.|File write and code execution are separate primitives.

ftp-chroot|F|F3|ftp|An FTP service confines users to a directory tree. What should assessment distinguish?|Filesystem confinement from file permissions and process privilege|Confinement from TLS certificate validity only|A directory tree from the user's browser viewport|A successful LIST from every possible escape|A restricted root can narrow paths, but writable objects, service code, and privilege still matter. A configured jail is not proof of complete containment.|Several controls jointly define file-service isolation.

smtp-order|F|F4|smtp|Why must an SMTP transaction identify recipients before submitting message data?|The envelope tells the server where delivery is requested|The DATA body automatically creates every recipient account|SMTP determines recipients only from the visible Subject|TLS certificates contain the recipient list|The SMTP envelope is distinct from message header fields. RCPT TO supplies recipient information for the transaction.|Envelope and message presentation are different layers.

smtp-rcpt|F|F4|smtp|A server accepts RCPT TO for an address. Why is that not definitive proof of a real mailbox?|Catch-all or deferred validation may accept unknown recipients|RCPT TO necessarily reveals the password|Acceptance always grants relay administration|The server cannot issue a later delivery failure|Recipient checks can be delayed or intentionally nondisclosing. Corroborate enumeration in the deployment context.|Admission and eventual delivery are different events.

smtp-starttls|F|F4|smtp|STARTTLS is advertised, but clients may continue without it. What must a confidentiality review assess?|Whether encryption is required and validated on relevant flows|Only whether the command appears in EHLO output|Only the server's banner capitalization|Only the mail message's HTML styling|Capability is not enforcement. Client/server policy and certificate validation determine the protected path.|Optional protection may not protect every transaction.

smtp-auth-relay|F|F4|smtp|An authenticated sender can relay mail, while unauthenticated third-party relay fails. Is that automatically an open relay?|No; authenticated relay can be intended policy|Yes; every onward mail transfer is an open relay|Yes; SMTP AUTH means every domain is anonymous|No; authentication proves every sender is trustworthy|Assess which principals and routes are authorized. Intended relay still needs account and abuse protections.|Relay policy must be evaluated by identity and destination.

nfs-all-squash|F|F5|nfs|How does all_squash differ from root_squash?|It maps all client user identities to anonymous identities|It gives every client identity UID 0|It encrypts all NFS responses|It prevents the NFS server from exporting files|Root squashing focuses on root; all_squash maps all users. Anonymous UID/GID and permissions then control access.|User mapping is not transport encryption.

nfs-nosuid-server|F|F5|nfs|Why check nosuid on the client mount when assessing a SUID file on NFS?|It can prevent honoring that file's privilege bits|It removes all file read permissions|It makes the server require Kerberos automatically|It changes every executable into a symbolic link|Mount options influence client execution semantics. Server exports and local mounts answer different questions.|Where a control is enforced matters.

noexec-interpreter|F|F5|unix|Why is noexec not a complete guarantee that readable script content cannot be used?|An interpreter may read it as data and execute its instructions|Noexec encrypts all script contents|All programs must ignore the mount option|Every readable script automatically has UID 0|Direct executable loading and interpreter reads are distinct paths. Other controls can constrain the latter.|Blocking direct execution is not universal prevention of interpretation.

rhosts-owner|F|F6|crest|Why do r-service trust-file ownership and mode checks matter?|They can prevent untrusted alteration of accepted trust rules|They encrypt all remote r-service traffic|They make every remote host's DNS answer signed|They change the trusted user's UID to zero|Host/user trust rules are only safe if their storage and validation are controlled. Encryption remains a separate issue.|Trust policy itself must be protected from modification.

hostname-trust|F|F6|crest|A legacy service authenticates by a remote hostname. What should a trust review examine?|How that name is resolved and bound to the connecting peer|Only the remote terminal's font size|Only whether the server uses a Unix path separator|Only the length of the visible account name|Name-based trust depends on trustworthy identity resolution and checks. A readable name is not a cryptographic peer identity.|Naming evidence and authenticated identity can differ.

x-cookie|F|F7|crest|What does X11 MIT-MAGIC-COOKIE-style access use as an authorization artifact?|A secret token supplied to the X server|The client's public DNS suffix alone|Every user's plaintext Unix password|The AP's wireless channel number|Cookie-based authorization differs from xhost-style host access. Token handling and transport security still matter.|An X authorization cookie is not an HTTP browser cookie.

x-listening|F|F7|crest|Why can xhost permissions be broad but network risk remain limited on a non-TCP-listening X server?|There may be no remote TCP route to that X service|Broad permissions automatically enable TLS|Every process is therefore free of local risk|The server must have disabled all input devices|Access policy and listening/reachability are separate dimensions. Local and forwarded clients may still be relevant.|A permissive rule needs an applicable path to have impact.

rpc-version|F|F8|crest|An RPC program number is registered with two protocol versions. What should a tester preserve?|Program, version, transport, and endpoint together|Only the highest numeric port|Only the host's friendly name|Only the user's terminal timestamp|RPC service selection includes program/version and transport. Different versions or paths can behave differently.|A service label can omit essential call-selection fields.

ssh-password-key|F|F9|sshauth|Disabling SSH password authentication leaves public-key authentication enabled. What changed?|One authentication mechanism was removed, not all login|The SSH transport became plaintext|Host-key validation became unnecessary|All authorized keys were revoked automatically|SSH supports several authentication methods. Review remaining keys, users, and policy as well as transport protection.|Disabling one method does not close every authentication route.

ssh-agent-forward|F|F9|sshcfg|Why can SSH agent forwarding be sensitive on an untrusted remote host?|The remote context may use the forwarded agent to request signatures|The private key must be transmitted in plaintext|The agent automatically changes the remote UID to zero|Forwarding signs every filesystem path permanently|Agent forwarding can expose signing capability while the connection exists. It does not necessarily copy the private key bytes.|Using a key's authority is different from possessing its file.
